story.headline: EU committee backs Swiss Bilaterals III
story.summary: The European Parliament's AFET committee approved the Switzerland-EU Bilaterals III package 53-3 on 10 September.
story.display_body: The European Parliament's foreign affairs committee (AFET) approved the Switzerland–EU "Bilaterals III" package on Thursday 10 September by 53 votes to 3. a lopsided endorsement on the EU side of a treaty that has yet to clear either parliament's plenary. Christophe Grudler, the French Renew MEP who is the file's rapporteur, called the vote an "étape importante" (important step) and said Brussels has no "plan B" if the deal fails. It follows the Swiss Council of States' committees, which on 4 September advanced the package on the domestic side but insisted it must pass a double majority of voters and cantons — so the ratification road still runs through a Swiss popular vote.
story.why: Bilaterals III governs free movement, the single market and research access that directly shape how people in Switzerland live, work and study with the EU; a strong committee signal in Brussels narrows the question to whether Swiss voters will ratify.

story.headline: Federal Council upholds 'Lex On'
story.summary: The Federal Council recommended rejecting two motions that sought to reverse the March Swissness amendment allowing the Swiss cross on goods made abroad.
story.display_body: The Federal Council has come out in favour of keeping the so-called "Lex On," recommending that parliament reject two motions that sought to undo a March amendment to the Swissness law. The change lets companies add the Swiss cross to labels such as "Swiss engineering" or "Swiss design" under certain conditions even when the product itself is made abroad — the Zurich brand On, whose shoes are manufactured in Asia, is the emblematic case. The government says it will accompany the looser practice with an "evaluation of the Swissness provisions." The two reversal motions came from PLR politician Daniela Schneeberger and Centre politician Fabio Regazzi; industrial circles, including in Vaud, have called the loosening a "dilution" of a "fabulous" asset and, in the sharpest framing, a "trahison" (betrayal) of firms that actually produce in Switzerland.
story.why: the Swiss cross is a paid-for marketing premium, and who may use it — genuine domestic manufacturers or brands that design here but build elsewhere — is a direct commercial fight over the value of "made in Switzerland."

story.headline: Explosion kills two at Ritom plant
story.summary: Two workers died in an explosion at the Ritom hydroelectric plant in Piotta, Ticino, on 9 September.
story.display_body: Two workers were killed in an explosion at the Ritom hydroelectric plant in Piotta, in Italian-speaking Ticino, shortly after 9:30 am on Wednesday 9 September. Ticino cantonal police, who described it as a "serious workplace accident," said a fire broke out inside the building and that, on a preliminary reconstruction, an explosion involving two workers left both dead of their injuries; one was a 55-year-old Swiss national and the other was still being formally identified. The 1917-era plant was undergoing a renovation in which new electrical machinery had recently been installed in the old section where the blast occurred. The cause remains under investigation.

story.headline: Swiss vacancy rate slips below 1%
story.summary: Switzerland's housing vacancy rate fell to 0.93% as of 1 June 2026, the Federal Statistical Office reported.
story.display_body: Switzerland's housing vacancy rate fell to 0.93% as of 1 June — 45,493 empty dwellings — the Federal Statistical Office (OFS/BFS) reported on Thursday. down 2,962 units (−6.1%) in a year and the continuation of a squeeze under way since 2021. Fifteen of 26 cantons now sit below the 1% mark economists treat as functional scarcity, with the tightest markets in Geneva, Zug and Zürich; vacancies fell in six of the seven large regions, Zürich being the lone slight riser. The tenants' association ASLOCA argued the remaining supply is skewed toward the high end and ill-suited to modest incomes, and renewed its call for regular, automatic rent checks.
story.why: a sub-1% vacancy rate means tighter searches and upward pressure on rents across most of the country — a direct cost-of-living squeeze for anyone moving or renewing a lease.

story.headline: Drone shuts Moldova airspace on Zelensky trip
story.summary: Moldova closed its airspace over a Russian drone incursion on 8 September, delaying Zelensky's flight to Norway; a claim the plane was 'almost hit' is disputed.
story.display_body: Moldova closed its airspace on Tuesday 8 September after a Russian drone incursion, delaying three departures including the flight carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to Norway. a Moldovan government spokesperson said. Moldovan police said a Russian drone crashed that day in a sunflower field in the Riscani district, sparking several fires. Zelensky was travelling to Oslo — where he ultimately arrived Tuesday — ahead of King Harald V's funeral. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said on Wednesday that a drone had "almost hit" Zelensky's plane; a source in the Ukrainian presidency told AFP that characterisation was "exaggerated," saying what occurred was an airspace alert rather than a near-miss on the aircraft. The severity is therefore disputed, though the airspace closure and drone crash are not.
story.why: Russian drones straying into Moldovan and Romanian (NATO) airspace are a recurring escalation risk on the war's western edge, independent of how close any one came to a head of state.

story.headline: Ukraine hits Russia's Arctic gas heartland
story.summary: Ukraine's deepest strike yet hit gas facilities near Novy Urengoy in the Russian Arctic on 9 September, as Russian attacks killed at least seven in Ukraine.
story.display_body: Ukraine carried out its deepest strike inside Russia to date on 9 September, sending drones more than 3,000 km to hit gas-processing facilities around Novy Urengoy in the Arctic Yamalo-Nenets region, while Russian attacks overnight into Thursday killed at least seven people in Ukraine. Kyiv's Special Operations Forces said they struck the Purovsky district; Russian officials said air defences repelled the raid but that falling debris started a fire, with no casualties reported. In Ukraine, four people were killed in Mykolaiv and three in a drone strike on a shopping centre in Sumy, officials said; Russia's defence ministry claimed the Mykolaiv strike hit a "drone warehouse" and said it also struck the port of Chornomorsk and vessels near Odesa.
story.why: reaching Russia's Arctic "gas capital" pushes Ukraine's long-range campaign into energy infrastructure thousands of kilometres from the front, widening the war's economic target set even as the civilian toll inside Ukraine continues.

story.headline: IAEA flags new North Korean enrichment plant
story.summary: The IAEA says North Korea built a new uranium-enrichment facility at Yongbyon and expanded its Kangson site.
story.display_body: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) says North Korea has built a new uranium-enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon complex and has expanded an annex at its Kangson site. according to a report dated 28 August and Director General Rafael Grossi's statement to the agency's Board of Governors on Monday 7 September. The new Yongbyon building could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades — the linked chains of centrifuges that spin uranium gas to raise its fissile U-235 content toward weapons grade — and the Kangson annex, built in 2024, has been operating since January. The IAEA, which has had no inspectors in the country since 2009, relied on satellite imagery and open-source material; Grossi called the apparent expansion of weapons-grade production "a cause for serious concern" and said it violates UN Security Council resolutions.
story.why: more enrichment capacity means more fissile material and, over time, more warheads — a steady, hard-to-verify growth in Pyongyang's arsenal that no inspection regime is currently watching from the ground.

story.headline: Hong Kong convicts WSJ publisher
story.summary: A Hong Kong court convicted Dow Jones Publishing (Asia) of deterring a reporter from a union role, acquitting it on a dismissal charge.
story.display_body: A Hong Kong court on Thursday 10 September convicted the publisher of The Wall Street Journal, Dow Jones Publishing Co. (Asia), of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade-union role. while acquitting it on a separate charge of dismissing her over the role. The private prosecution was brought by former WSJ journalist Selina Cheng, chair of the Hong Kong Journalists Association, who lost her job in July 2024; Principal Magistrate David Cheung found sufficient reasonable doubt on the dismissal count but convicted on the first.
story.why: the ruling lands amid sustained pressure on press freedom and union activity in Hong Kong, and tests how far the city's labour law protects journalists who organise.
